heading: What is a Database & DBMS
subheading: Organized data storage and the software that manages it
description:
Data refers to raw facts and figures. When data is processed and given context, it becomes information.

A Database is an organized, consistent, and logical collection of data that can be easily accessed, managed, and updated. Data is stored in tables — rows (tuples) represent individual records, and columns (attributes) represent the properties of each record.

A DBMS (Database Management System) is the software that enables users to create, manage, and interact with databases. It provides tools for inserting, updating, deleting, and querying data while handling security, concurrency, and integrity behind the scenes.

Why DBMS over traditional file systems?
Traditional file-based storage suffers from several problems that DBMS solves:
• **Data Redundancy** — files often contain duplicate data. DBMS eliminates this through normalization.
• **Data Inconsistency** — updating one copy but not others leads to conflicting data.
• No Concurrent Access — file systems lock entire files, blocking other users. DBMS allows multiple users to work simultaneously.
• No Data Integrity — file systems have no built-in rules to enforce valid data.
• Poor Security — file systems lack fine-grained access control.
• No Atomicity — if a file operation fails midway, data is left in a corrupt state.

Types of DBMS:
• **Hierarchical** — data organized in a tree structure (parent-child). A child can have only one parent.
• Network — data organized as a graph. A child can have multiple parents.
• **Relational (RDBMS)** — data stored in tables with rows and columns, linked through keys. Most widely used (e.g., MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle).
• **Object-Oriented** — data stored as objects with attributes and methods, similar to OOP.

heading: Schema, Architecture & Data Abstraction
subheading: How databases are structured and how complexity is hidden from users
description:
**Schema vs Instance:**
• Schema — the structure or blueprint of the database (table definitions, column types, constraints). It rarely changes once designed.
• Instance — the actual data stored in the database at any given moment. It changes constantly as data is inserted, updated, or deleted.

**Database Architecture:**
• 2-Tier Architecture — the client application communicates directly with the database. Simple and low maintenance, but lacks security and scalability.
• 3-Tier Architecture — a middle layer (application/business logic server) sits between the client and the database. Provides better security, scalability, and separation of concerns. This is the standard for modern web applications.

**Levels of Data Abstraction:**
• Physical Level (lowest) — describes how data is physically stored on disk. Managed by the DBMS internally; hidden from users and developers.
• Logical/Conceptual Level (middle) — describes what data is stored and the relationships between tables. This is where developers and DBAs work.
• View/External Level (highest) — describes only a portion of the database relevant to a specific user or application. Different users can see different views of the same data.

**DBA (Database Administrator):**
The person responsible for managing, securing, maintaining, and optimizing the database to ensure smooth operation. They handle backups, recovery, performance tuning, and access control.

heading: ER Model & Relationships
subheading: Designing databases by modeling real-world entities and their connections
description:
The Entity-Relationship (ER) Model is a visual approach to database design. It represents real-world objects as entities and the connections between them as relationships.

Key concepts:
• Entity — a real-world object that can be uniquely identified. For example: a student, an employee, or a product.
• Entity Type — a category of entities that share the same attributes. For example: "Student" is an entity type with attributes like student_id, name, and email.
• Entity Set — the collection of all entities of a particular entity type in the database.
• Attributes — the properties that describe an entity (e.g., name, age, email).

Types of Relationships between tables:
• One-to-One — each row in Table A is linked to exactly one row in Table B. Example: one person has one passport.
• One-to-Many — one row in Table A can be linked to many rows in Table B. Example: one department has many employees.
• Many-to-Many — multiple rows in Table A can be linked to multiple rows in Table B. Example: students enroll in multiple courses, and each course has multiple students. This is typically implemented using a junction table.

The ER diagram is drawn during the design phase before any tables are created. It helps visualize the structure, identify relationships, and catch design issues early.

heading: SQL Fundamentals & Commands
subheading: The standard language for interacting with relational databases
description:
SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language used to communicate with relational databases. It allows you to create, read, update, and delete data, as well as define and control the database structure.

SQL commands are organized into four categories:

• **DDL (Data Definition Language)** — defines the structure of the database.
  Commands: CREATE (create tables/databases), ALTER (modify structure), DROP (delete tables/databases), TRUNCATE (remove all rows from a table), RENAME.

• **DML (Data Manipulation Language)** — works with the data inside tables.
  Commands: SELECT (retrieve data), INSERT (add new rows), UPDATE (modify existing rows), DELETE (remove specific rows).

• **DCL (Data Control Language)** — manages user permissions and access.
  Commands: GRANT (give permissions), REVOKE (remove permissions).

• **TCL (Transaction Control Language)** — manages transactions.
  Commands: COMMIT (save changes permanently), ROLLBACK (undo changes), SAVEPOINT (set a checkpoint within a transaction).

**DELETE vs TRUNCATE:**
• DELETE removes specific rows based on a WHERE clause, maintains a log, can be rolled back, but is slower.
• TRUNCATE removes all rows at once without logging individual deletions, cannot be reliably rolled back, and is much faster.

Common SQL terms:
• Table — organized data stored in rows and columns.
• Field — a column in a table, representing a specific attribute.
• Constraint — a rule applied to a column (e.g., NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY).

heading: Keys in a Database
subheading: Uniquely identifying records and establishing relationships between tables
description:
Keys are columns (or combinations of columns) used to uniquely identify rows and define relationships between tables.

• **Primary Key** — uniquely identifies every row in a table. Cannot be NULL, and each table can have only one primary key.
• **Foreign Key** — a column in one table that references the primary key of another table. It creates a link between the two tables and enforces referential integrity.
• **Unique Key** — similar to a primary key in that it enforces uniqueness, but it allows one NULL value. A table can have multiple unique keys.
• **Candidate Key** — any column (or set of columns) that could serve as the primary key. One candidate key is chosen as the primary key; the rest become alternate keys.
• **Alternate Key** — all candidate keys that were not chosen as the primary key.
• **Super Key** — any set of columns that can uniquely identify a row. Every primary key and candidate key is a super key, but a super key can include extra columns.
• **Composite Key** — a key made up of two or more columns that together uniquely identify a row. Used when no single column is unique on its own.

Relationship between key types:
A super key can be a composite key. Every candidate key is a super key. The primary key is a special candidate key chosen to be the main identifier.

heading: SQL Joins
subheading: Combining data from multiple tables based on related columns
description:
A JOIN combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them. Joins are the backbone of relational queries.

Types of Joins:
• **INNER JOIN** — returns only the rows where there is a match in both tables. If a row in Table A has no corresponding row in Table B, it is excluded.
• **LEFT (OUTER) JOIN** — returns all rows from the left table and the matching rows from the right table. If there is no match, NULL values are returned for the right table's columns.
• **RIGHT (OUTER) JOIN** — returns all rows from the right table and the matching rows from the left table. If there is no match, NULL values are returned for the left table's columns.
• **FULL (OUTER) JOIN** — returns all rows from both tables. Where there is no match, NULL values fill in the missing side.
• **CROSS JOIN** — returns the Cartesian product of both tables (every row in A paired with every row in B). Rarely used in practice.
• **SELF JOIN** — a table is joined with itself. Useful when rows within the same table have a hierarchical or comparative relationship.

Self Join example — finding employees and their supervisors:
SELECT A.emp_name AS Employee, B.emp_name AS Supervisor
FROM employee A, employee B
WHERE A.emp_sup = B.emp_id;

Here, the employee table is aliased as both A and B to compare rows within the same table.

heading: Normalization
subheading: Organizing tables to eliminate redundancy and prevent data anomalies
description:
Normalization is the process of structuring a relational database to reduce data redundancy and prevent anomalies during insertion, update, and deletion.

**Anomalies that normalization solves:**
• **Insertion Anomaly** — you cannot store one piece of information without also inserting unrelated information.
• **Update Anomaly** — updating one piece of data requires changing it in multiple places.
• **Deletion Anomaly** — deleting one piece of data accidentally removes other unrelated information.

**Functional Dependency:** A relationship where one attribute uniquely determines another (e.g., student_id → student_name).

**Normal Forms:**
• **1NF (First Normal Form)** — every column must contain only atomic (single) values. No repeating groups. Each record must be uniquely identifiable.
• **2NF (Second Normal Form)** — must be in 1NF. No partial dependency — every non-key attribute must depend on the entire primary key, not just a part of it.
• **3NF (Third Normal Form)** — must be in 2NF. No transitive dependency — non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes. Every non-key attribute must depend directly on the primary key.
• **BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form / 3.5NF)** — must be in 3NF. For every functional dependency A → B, A must be a super key. Even prime attributes must be derived from a key.

**Denormalization:**
The reverse of normalization — intentionally combining tables to speed up read-heavy queries. It reintroduces some redundancy but improves query performance by reducing the number of joins needed. Common in data warehouses and reporting systems.

heading: Indexing & B-Trees
subheading: Speeding up data retrieval by avoiding full table scans
description:
An index is a data structure that speeds up searches in a database table. Without an index, the database must scan every row (full table scan) to find a match, which is extremely slow on large tables.

Types of Indexing:
• **Primary Index** — built on the primary key of a sorted table. The index table has two columns: the key value and a pointer to the data block. It is a sparse index (one entry per data block).
• **Clustered Index** — built on a non-key attribute. Data is physically sorted by the indexed column. Groups of rows with the same value share an index entry.
• **Secondary Index** — used when data is not sorted by the indexed column. The index itself is sorted, but the underlying data is not. Every row gets an entry in the index (dense index).
• **Multi-Level Indexing** — when the index itself becomes too large to fit in memory, another level of indexing is created on top of it. Managed using B-Trees and B+ Trees.

**B-Tree:**
A self-balancing tree structure where each node contains keys, data pointers (pointing to actual records), and block pointers (pointing to child nodes). Data pointers are spread across all nodes, which means searches may need to traverse internal nodes.

**B+ Tree (preferred in databases):**
An improvement over B-Trees where data pointers exist only in the leaf nodes. Internal nodes contain only keys and child pointers. Leaf nodes are linked together using record pointers, making range queries and sequential access extremely efficient. This is why B+ Trees are the standard index structure in most relational databases.

heading: Transactions & ACID Properties
subheading: Ensuring data integrity when multiple operations must succeed or fail together
description:
A transaction is a set of logically related database operations that must be treated as a single unit. Either all operations succeed (commit), or none of them take effect (rollback).

**ACID Properties:**
• **Atomicity** — all or nothing. If any part of the transaction fails, the entire transaction is rolled back. The database is never left in a half-finished state.
• **Consistency** — a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another. All integrity constraints, rules, and triggers are satisfied before and after the transaction.
• **Isolation** — concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other. Each transaction executes as if it were the only one running. The final result is the same as if all transactions had run sequentially.
• **Durability** — once a transaction is committed, the changes are permanent and survive system crashes, power failures, or restarts.

Schedules:
• **Serial Schedule** — transactions run one after another, with no interleaving. Simple and correct, but slow.
• **Non-Serial Schedule** — operations from different transactions are interleaved for better performance. Must be carefully managed to avoid inconsistencies.

Serializability:
A non-serial schedule is considered correct (serializable) if its outcome is equivalent to some serial schedule. This ensures that concurrent execution produces the same result as sequential execution.

heading: Concurrency Control & Locks
subheading: Managing simultaneous access to prevent data corruption
description:
Concurrency control ensures that multiple users or processes can read and write to the database simultaneously without causing data inconsistencies or conflicts.

Why it is needed:
Without concurrency control, two transactions modifying the same data at the same time could overwrite each other's changes, read partially updated data, or leave the database in an inconsistent state.

Locking Mechanism:
A lock is a mechanism that prevents other transactions from accessing the same data while one transaction is working on it.

• **Shared Lock (S-lock / Read Lock)** — acquired when a transaction wants to read data. Multiple transactions can hold shared locks on the same data simultaneously, since reading does not change anything.
• **Exclusive Lock (X-lock / Write Lock)** — acquired when a transaction wants to modify data. Only one transaction can hold an exclusive lock on a piece of data at a time. No other transaction can read or write that data until the lock is released.

Isolation Levels (from least to most strict):
• **Read Uncommitted** — transactions can see uncommitted changes from other transactions (dirty reads possible).
• **Read Committed** — transactions only see committed data. Prevents dirty reads.
• **Repeatable Read** — guarantees that if a row is read twice within a transaction, it will return the same value. Prevents non-repeatable reads.
• **Serializable** — the strictest level. Transactions are fully isolated as if they ran sequentially. Prevents phantom reads but has the highest performance cost.

heading: OLAP vs OLTP
subheading: Analytical queries vs day-to-day transactions — two different workloads
description:
**OLTP (Online Transaction Processing):**
Designed for day-to-day transactional operations — the kind of queries your application runs constantly.
• Short, simple queries (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT by ID).
• High volume of small transactions.
• Optimized for fast reads and writes.
• Examples: banking transactions, e-commerce orders, ticket bookings.

**OLAP (Online Analytical Processing):**
Designed for complex analytical queries that process large volumes of historical data.
• Long, complex queries involving aggregations, joins across many tables, and GROUP BY operations.
• Used for reporting, dashboards, business intelligence, and trend analysis.
• Not needed for day-to-day operations.
• Examples: sales trend analysis, quarterly revenue reports, customer behavior analytics.

**Data Warehousing:**
A data warehouse is a centralized storage system that collects and integrates large volumes of historical data from multiple sources (transactional databases, logs, APIs). It is optimized for OLAP queries rather than transactional processing.

**Data Mining:**
The process of discovering hidden patterns, trends, and relationships from large datasets using statistical and machine learning techniques. It operates on data stored in data warehouses to extract actionable business insights.

heading: NoSQL Databases
subheading: Flexible, scalable alternatives to relational databases for unstructured data
description:
NoSQL ("Not Only SQL") databases are designed to handle large volumes of unstructured or semi-structured data that do not fit neatly into relational tables with fixed schemas.

Four main types:
• **Document Databases** — store data as JSON/BSON documents. Each document can have a different structure. Example: MongoDB, CouchDB.
• **Key-Value Stores** — store data as simple key-value pairs. Optimized for extremely fast reads and writes. Example: Redis, DynamoDB.
• **Column-Family Stores** — organize data by columns instead of rows. Efficient for querying large datasets with specific column patterns. Example: Cassandra, HBase.
• **Graph Databases** — store data as nodes and edges, optimized for complex relationships. Example: Neo4j, Amazon Neptune.

Advantages:
• Dynamic schema — no fixed structure; adapts to changing data models without migrations.
• Horizontal scalability — scales out by adding more nodes, handling massive traffic easily.
• High availability — built-in replication ensures data survives node failures.
• Performance — optimized for high-volume reads and writes.

Disadvantages:
• Not fully ACID-compliant — may sacrifice consistency for performance and availability.
• No standardization — each NoSQL database has its own query language and behavior.
• Weak support for complex queries — not ideal for multi-table joins or complex analytics.
• Management complexity — backup, monitoring, and administration can be more challenging.

**CAP Theorem:**
In any distributed system, you can guarantee at most two of the following three properties:
• **Consistency** — every read returns the most recent write.
• Availability — every request gets a response, even if some nodes are down.
• Partition Tolerance — the system continues to operate even if network communication between nodes fails.

Since network partitions are unavoidable in distributed systems, you must choose between consistency (CP systems like MongoDB) or availability (AP systems like Cassandra).

heading: Sharding & Scaling
subheading: Distributing data across multiple machines to handle growth
description:
**Sharding (Data Partitioning):**
Sharding is a database architecture pattern where a large dataset is split into smaller chunks (shards), and each shard is stored on a separate database server. Every row appears in exactly one shard, and all shards share the same schema.

**Types of Sharding:**
• **Hash-Based Sharding** — a hash function is applied to a column value (shard key, e.g., user ID) to determine which shard the data belongs to. Distributes data evenly but makes range queries difficult.
• **Range-Based (Horizontal) Sharding** — data is split based on value ranges (e.g., customers A–M on Shard 1, N–Z on Shard 2). Simple but can lead to uneven distribution if ranges are not chosen carefully.
• **Vertical Sharding** — different columns of a table are split into different shards. Each shard holds a subset of attributes. Useful when some columns are accessed far more frequently than others.
• **Directory-Based Sharding** — a lookup table maps each record to its shard. Flexible but adds the overhead of maintaining the lookup service.

**Scaling:**
• **Vertical Scaling (Scale Up)** — adding more power (CPU, RAM, storage) to the existing server. Simpler and cheaper initially, but has a physical limit.
• **Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out)** — adding more servers to distribute the load. More complex to implement but virtually unlimited in capacity. This is the standard approach for large-scale applications.

Sharding enables horizontal scaling for databases that would otherwise become too large for a single server.
